chapters.name: Chapter 1: How crypto and blockchain work

lessons.title: Lesson 1: What a blockchain is
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Explain a blockchain in plain words using a simple picture.
This lesson builds toward: Using the shared-notebook picture, you will explain what a blockchain is, including the words block, chain and decentralized, in two or three plain sentences with no mistakes about how records are kept.
Picture a notebook of payments that thousands of computers each keep a copy of. Every few minutes a new page of payments is added. Each page is locked to the page before it with a kind of math fingerprint, so if someone changes an old page, every other copy shows it does not match.
That shared notebook is a blockchain. Each page is a block, and the pages are chained together in order. No single bank or company keeps the notebook; the network of computers does. This is called decentralized.
Because of this design, a payment written into the blockchain is very hard to change or undo. Most blockchains are also public: anyone can look up the payments, even if the names behind them are not shown.
Words to know:
- Blockchain: a shared record of transactions, kept by many computers, where each new block is linked to the one before it.
- Block: a group of transactions added to the blockchain together.
- Decentralized: run by a network of many computers instead of one bank or company.
- Ledger: a record of payments, like an account book.
Try it now: Explain a blockchain to someone (or out loud to yourself) using the shared-notebook picture. Include the words block, chain and decentralized.
You can now explain what a blockchain is and why its records are hard to change.

check.q: In the shared-notebook picture, what is a block?
options: The whole notebook
The bank that owns the notebook
One page of payments added to the notebook
A password for the notebook
check.why: Each page of payments is a block, and the pages are chained together in order.

check.q: Someone tells you they can quietly change an old payment on a public blockchain. What would you think?
options: It is very unlikely, because the other copies would not match
It is easy, because one company keeps the notebook
It is normal, because blockchains are private
It is true, because blocks are not linked
check.why: Each block is locked to the one before it, so a changed page would not match the other copies.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: What a cryptocurrency is
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Explain what a cryptocurrency is and how it differs from dollars in a bank.
This lesson builds toward: Without notes, you will explain what a cryptocurrency is and list how it differs from money in an insured bank account, naming at least three differences, including that crypto payments usually cannot be reversed.
A cryptocurrency (crypto) is digital money recorded on a blockchain. Bitcoin was the first; there are now thousands, such as Ether. A stablecoin is a kind of crypto designed to stay close to the value of a regular currency like the US dollar, but it can still fail.
Crypto is not issued by a government, and its price goes up and down with what people are willing to pay. Prices can rise or fall a lot in one day.
Crypto payments are different from card payments. The FTC says crypto payments do not come with the legal protections that credit and debit cards have, and they usually cannot be reversed. Money in crypto is also not the same as money in an insured bank account.
Words to know:
- Cryptocurrency (crypto): digital money recorded on a blockchain, like Bitcoin or Ether.
- Stablecoin: crypto designed to stay close to the value of a regular currency, such as the US dollar.
- Volatile: a price that can go up or down a lot, quickly.
Official sources:
- FTC: What to know about cryptocurrency and scams
Try it now: Write three differences between paying with a debit card and paying with crypto. Use the FTC page in this lesson's sources to check your answer.
You can now explain what a cryptocurrency is and how it is different from bank money and card payments.

options: Paper money from a government
Digital money recorded on a blockchain
A savings account at a bank
A gift card from a store
check.why: Crypto is digital money recorded on a blockchain, not issued by a government.

check.q: A seller asks you to pay in crypto instead of with your credit card. What should you keep in mind?
options: Crypto has more legal protection than a card
Crypto payments are always easy to cancel
Crypto is insured just like a bank account
Crypto payments usually cannot be reversed if something goes wrong
check.why: The FTC says crypto payments lack card protections and usually cannot be reversed.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Wallets, keys and exchanges
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Explain how crypto is stored and sent, and what must never be shared.
This lesson builds toward: Given the words wallet, public address, recovery phrase and exchange, you will describe what each one is and identify which ones must never be shared, with each one described correctly and the recovery phrase and private key always kept secret.
Crypto is kept in a wallet: an app, website or small device that holds your keys. The public address is like an account number you can give someone so they can send you crypto. The private key, often shown as a recovery phrase (a list of 12 or 24 words), is like the master key. Whoever has it controls the crypto.
Never share a recovery phrase or private key with anyone: not support staff, not a "helper", not an app, not an AI assistant. A real company will never ask for it. If you lose it, the crypto may be gone forever.
An exchange is a company where people buy, sell and hold crypto. Exchanges can be hacked or go out of business. In the United States, check whether a company is registered and read its complaints before trusting it; regulators such as the SEC and CFTC publish warnings.
Words to know:
- Wallet: an app or device that holds the keys to your crypto.
- Public address: a code others use to send you crypto, like an account number.
- Private key / recovery phrase: the secret that controls the crypto; never share it.
- Exchange: a company where people buy, sell and hold crypto.
Official sources:
- FTC: What to know about cryptocurrency and scams
- SEC: Submit a tip or complaint
- CFTC: Submit a complaint
Try it now: Write one sentence each: what a public address is, what a recovery phrase is, and what you would say if a "support agent" asked for your recovery phrase.
You can now explain how crypto is stored and sent and why a recovery phrase must never be shared.

options: A greeting you send with a payment
The name of an exchange
Your public address
A list of 12 or 24 words that controls your crypto
check.why: Whoever has the recovery phrase controls the crypto, like a master key.

check.q: A friend wants to send you crypto and asks what to use. What would you give them?
options: Your recovery phrase
Your private key
Your public address
Your bank PIN
check.why: The public address is like an account number and is safe to share for receiving crypto.

lessons.title: Lesson 4: The real risks
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Name the main risks of holding or receiving crypto.
This lesson builds toward: Without notes, you will name the four main risks of crypto and one way to protect yourself from each, with all four risks (price, loss, company and scam) named correctly.
Price risk: crypto prices can drop sharply, and nobody can promise they will come back. Never put in money you need for rent, food, bills or medicine.
Loss risk: if you lose your recovery phrase, or send crypto to the wrong address, it is usually gone. Payments usually cannot be reversed.
Company risk: exchanges and apps can be hacked or close down. The FDIC says crypto assets are not covered by FDIC deposit insurance, which covers only deposits at FDIC-insured banks. Scam risk: crypto is a favorite payment method of scammers because it is fast and hard to get back.
This course does not tell you whether to buy. If you are thinking about it, talk with a licensed financial professional you choose yourself, and read the official warnings first.
Words to know:
- Risk: the chance of losing money or something going wrong.
- FDIC insurance: US government protection for money in insured bank deposit accounts; it does not cover crypto.
Official sources:
- FTC: What to know about cryptocurrency and scams
- FDIC: Understanding deposit insurance
Try it now: Write the four risks in your own words: price, loss, company and scam. For each one, write one way a person could protect themselves.
You can now name the main risks of crypto and explain why money you need should never be put at risk.

check.q: What is price risk with crypto?
options: The price can drop sharply and nobody can promise it will come back
The price is fixed by the government
The price only goes up over time
The price is the same as the dollar every day
check.why: Crypto prices can drop sharply, so never put in money you need for bills.

check.q: Your cousin wants to put this month's rent money into crypto. What would you tell them?
options: Go ahead; prices always come back
Do not use money you need for rent, food, bills or medicine
Put it on an exchange because exchanges are insured
Send it quickly before the price changes
check.why: Prices can fall a lot, so money needed for basics should never go into crypto.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Spotting crypto scams
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Check a crypto offer or message against the warning signs of a scam.
This lesson builds toward: Given a real crypto ad, message or post, you will check it against the warning signs of a crypto scam and choose a safe response, marking every warning sign it shows and choosing to stop, not pay and talk to someone you trust.
The FTC lists signs of crypto scams. Only scammers demand payment in crypto, especially up front or to "protect" your money. Only scammers guarantee profits or big, quick returns. Celebrity endorsements can be fake.
Watch for a new online friend or romantic partner who starts giving investment tips or asks for crypto. Watch for calls or texts claiming to be from a government agency, bank or utility that say you owe money or your account is frozen and you must pay in crypto or at a crypto ATM.
Also watch for jobs that ask you to pay a fee in crypto, and for emails threatening to share private things unless you pay in crypto. When you see any of these, stop. Do not pay, do not click, and talk to someone you trust.
Step by step:
- Does it ask you to pay in crypto or use a crypto ATM?
- Does it promise guaranteed or quick profits?
- Did it come from a new online friend, a romantic contact or a stranger?
- Does it rush you or threaten you?
- Any yes: stop, do not pay, and check with someone you trust.
Words to know:
- Scam: a trick to steal money or information.
- Crypto ATM: a machine that turns cash into crypto; scammers often tell victims to use one.
- Romance scam: a scam where someone builds an online relationship to get money.
Official sources:
- FTC: What to know about cryptocurrency and scams
Try it now: Find one crypto ad, message or social media post. Go through the five check questions and write down every warning sign it shows.
You can now check a crypto offer or message against the warning signs and stop before paying.

check.q: Which of these is a warning sign of a crypto scam?
options: A bank letter you asked for
A friend explaining what a blockchain is
A demand to pay in crypto up front to protect your money
A news story about Bitcoin's price
check.why: Only scammers demand payment in crypto up front or to "protect" your money.

check.q: A text says your bank account is frozen and you must pay at a crypto ATM today. What would you do?
options: Go to the crypto ATM right away
Reply with your account number
Click the link in the text to check
Stop, do not pay or click, and talk to someone you trust
check.why: Claims that you owe money and must pay in crypto are a scam sign, so stop and do not pay.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Reporting fraud and helping others
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: List where to report a crypto scam and what to write down.
This lesson builds toward: Given a crypto scam that happened to you or someone you know, you will list the official places to report it and the details to write down, naming at least two official reporting sites and at least four details to record.
If you or someone you know was targeted, report it. The FTC lists these places: the FTC at ReportFraud.ftc.gov, the CFTC at cftc.gov/complaint, the SEC at sec.gov/tcr, the FBI's Internet Crime Complaint Center (IC3) at ic3.gov, and the crypto exchange or app used to send the money.
Write down what happened: dates, the amount, the wallet address or transaction ID, the names and phone numbers the scammer used, and screenshots of messages. Do not send more money to anyone who promises to "recover" your lost crypto; that is often a second scam.
Talk about scams with family and friends, especially older relatives and young people who are new to money apps. A short conversation can stop a loss.
Step by step:
- Stop all payments and contact with the scammer.
- Write down dates, amounts, wallet addresses, transaction IDs, names and numbers.
- Save screenshots.
- Report at ReportFraud.ftc.gov and ic3.gov, plus the SEC or CFTC if it was an investment.
- Tell the exchange or app you used.
- Ignore anyone who offers to recover your money for a fee.
Words to know:
- Transaction ID: the code that identifies one crypto payment on the blockchain.
- IC3: the FBI's Internet Crime Complaint Center, which takes reports of online crime.
- Recovery scam: a second scam that promises to get your lost money back for a fee.
Official sources:
- FTC: What to know about cryptocurrency and scams
- FTC: ReportFraud
- FBI Internet Crime Complaint Center (IC3)
- SEC: Submit a tip or complaint
- CFTC: Submit a complaint
Try it now: Final task: make your one-page crypto safety card (what blockchain and crypto are, three risks, four scam signs, where to report). Then mark the warning signs in one real crypto ad or message.
You can now report a crypto scam to the right places and help family and friends avoid one.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds What blockchain and crypto are The two sentences are missing, wrong or copied without explaining. Two plain sentences correctly say what a blockchain and a cryptocurrency are. Also says why crypto payments are hard to undo. Three risks Fewer than three risks, or a risk is wrong. Three correct risks from price, loss, company and scam. Each risk has one way to protect yourself. Keys and recovery phrase The card does not say to keep the recovery phrase secret, or says it is safe to share. The card says never to share the recovery phrase or private key with anyone. Also says the public address is the only thing safe to share for receiving crypto. Four scam warning signs Fewer than four signs, or a sign is wrong. Four correct warning signs, and the real ad or message is marked with every sign it shows. Also writes the safe response: stop, do not pay or click, and talk to someone you trust. Where to report No official reporting place, or an unofficial one. At least two official places to report, such as ReportFraud.ftc.gov and ic3.gov. Also lists the details to write down and warns about recovery scams. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part of the card and check it again.

check.q: Which of these is an official place to report crypto fraud in the US?
options: A comment on the scammer's social media post
The FBI's Internet Crime Complaint Center at ic3.gov
A stranger who says they can recover your money
A crypto chat group
check.why: IC3 at ic3.gov is one of the official places the FTC lists for reporting.

check.q: Your neighbor was scammed and wants to report it. What would you help them do first?
options: Write down dates, amounts, the wallet address or transaction ID, and save screenshots
Delete every message from the scammer
Pay a recovery service to get the money back
Send the scammer more crypto to close the account
check.why: Those details help the agencies and the exchange follow up on the report.
